clue.text: I caught ball

indicators.note: to catch what someone says is to hear it, so the sound of the word counts rather than its spelling

parts.note: the pronoun and the organ of sight are pronounced identically

explanation.surface: A fielder proudly reports taking a catch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' reads as a cricket dismissal, but here it means heard. The ball is the eyeball.
explanation.definitionFit: The eyeball is a spherical organ, so the organ of sight can be called a ball.

clue.text: Outperform skinny swimmer going about 90

indicators.note: going about something means travelling around it, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: an eel is a long thin fish
XC is 90 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A slim competitor in the pool is doing about ninety and beating everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: The swimmer is a fish, not an athlete; the eel wraps around the Roman ninety.
explanation.definitionFit: To excel is to do better than others, which is what outperforming means as a verb.

clue.text: Setter climbs church next to green high-rise

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: the setter refers to themselves as me

indicators.note: high can mean intoxicated, and drunk letters lose their proper order

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
taken as written

explanation.surface: The puzzle compiler goes up a church tower beside the village green and looks at a tower block.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High-rise' looks like a tall building, but the hyphen hides two jobs: 'high' scrambles the church and green, and 'rise' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A rise into view or prominence is an emergence, so the noun rise can stand for coming out or appearing.

clue.text: Stirrer stirring in tea leaves originally from the ground

indicators.note: stirring mixes things up, so these letters are churned into a new order
one thing placed in another sits inside it, so these letters go into the middle of the others

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: originally points to how a word begins, so only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of leaves
the seven letters of this word rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone stirs a teapot and looks at the leaves settling at the bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stirrer' looks like the teaspoon in the scene, but it is the fodder; 'in' puts its rearranged letters inside the tea and leaf, not the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: Terrestrial describes things belonging to the earth or land, as opposed to the sea, air or space.

clue.text: One of the 22 players snubbed by Liverpool's no. 1

indicators.note: snub-nosed means having a short nose, so the word loses its tip at the end

parts.note: a team of players, with its last letter cut off

indicators.note: number one in a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: first letter of Liverpool

explanation.surface: A footballer in a match is cold-shouldered by Liverpool's top player.
explanation.walkthrough: '22' is not two teams of eleven but a cross-reference to 22 Down, DUCKS; the surface makes it look like the players on a football pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: The teal is a small dabbling freshwater bird, one species among the many wild ducks.

clue.text: Poke around the middle of crossbill's nest

indicators.note: something around another encloses it, so one set of letters wraps the other

parts.note: to root is to poke about or rummage

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the fifth of nine letters

explanation.surface: Someone pokes around inside a crossbill's nest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poke around' looks like a single phrasal verb; it is the verb plus the containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A roost is a place where birds settle to rest, close enough in sense to a nest.

clue.text: 'Stayin' Alive' excites one headed to dance

indicators.note: headed here means beheaded, so the word loses its first letter
dancing letters move about and change places

parts.note: taken as written
the word with its first letter removed

explanation.surface: The Bee Gees disco hit gets someone up to dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The song title is the definition read literally: staying alive is existing. 'One' is not I here but the word itself, beheaded.
explanation.definitionFit: Existence is the state of being alive and continuing to live, which is what staying alive describes.

clue.text: Memorials to mark devout person's remains outside

indicators.note: being outside something means surrounding it, so these letters enclose the others

parts.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for the German mark
a skeleton's remains
a saint, abbreviated ST

explanation.surface: Headstones commemorate a pious person whose remains lie outside the church.
explanation.walkthrough: The saint's 's means 'is', so the saint is what the bones sit outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Tombstones are carved stones set over graves to commemorate the dead, a kind of memorial.

clue.text: Some purblind ring-tailed lemur

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only part of it, so the letters are found inside the words

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second
surface padding, completing the name of a real lemur species

explanation.surface: A half-blind ring-tailed lemur.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen joins 'ring' to 'tailed' in the surface, but the hidden letters straddle 'purblind' and 'ring'. The ring-tailed lemur is a real species, though not this one.
explanation.definitionFit: The indri is the largest living lemur, found in Madagascar.

clue.text: New in — boy's head is wider than it is tall

indicators.note: placing one thing in another puts it inside, so this letter goes into the next word

parts.note: boy is lad, and the 's adds S
N is the abbreviation for new
a cape is a headland

explanation.surface: A boy's newly drawn head comes out wider than it is tall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' is a headland jutting into the sea, not a part of the body.
explanation.definitionFit: Landscape orientation, for a page or picture, is the format where the width exceeds the height.

clue.text: Designer carries 21 tops for idle ushers marshalling funeral venue

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it within, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a designer is a creator
21 Down is METRE, abbreviated M

indicators.note: the tops of words are their first letters, so only those are kept

parts.note: first letters of the three words

explanation.surface: An event designer arranges the order of service while idle ushers are marshalled at a funeral venue.
explanation.walkthrough: '21' refers to the answer at 21 Down, the unit METRE, which shortens to M.
explanation.definitionFit: A crematorium is the building where bodies are burned, typically with a chapel for the service, so it is a funeral venue.

clue.text: Kelly's back room

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters are read from the end

parts.note: Ned Kelly was the Australian outlaw

explanation.surface: A person named Kelly has a room at the back of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: Kelly is the surname of Ned Kelly, the famous Australian bushranger, so his first name is the piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A den is a small private room in a house, used for relaxing or working, so it counts as a room.

clue.text: Stages on which Sir Ralph Richardson stood

definitions.meaning: first meaning: sections of a journey or competition

definitions.text: on which Sir Ralph Richardson stood
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the limbs anyone stands on, actor or not

explanation.surface: The theatre boards where the great actor Sir Ralph Richardson once performed.
explanation.walkthrough: Richardson was a celebrated English stage actor, so 'Stages' seems to mean theatres; in fact he stood on what everyone stands on.
explanation.definitionFit: A journey or relay is divided into separate parts each called a leg, and people stand upright on their two lower limbs.

clue.text: Facts say syphilis gets caught by 'resting' close to others

indicators.note: something caught is held inside its catcher, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: static means at rest, not moving
syphilis is an example of a sexually transmitted infection, STI

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is kept

parts.note: last letter of others

explanation.surface: Data show that syphilis spreads when people rest close to others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks syphilis as an example of a category, so the piece is the category's abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Statistics are numerical data collected and presented as facts about a population.

clue.text: Charged issue agitating the leaders of Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan and north Asia

indicators.note: agitating something shakes it about, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: leaders come at the front, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

parts.note: first letters of the two countries
first letter of north
taken as written

explanation.surface: A contentious political question is stirring up the heads of state in Central Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests 'the' belongs to 'leaders', but it is fodder too, and the leader selection stops before Asia, which goes in whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Assisted dying is a fiercely debated moral and legal question, so it is an emotionally charged topic.

clue.text: African people in bar nicked beer barrel

indicators.note: a nick is a small cut, so the word has its end trimmed

parts.note: to bar is to ban
a tun is a large beer cask, here with its last letter cut

explanation.surface: Some African drinkers in a pub have stolen a barrel of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nicked' looks like slang for stole, but it means cut short. 'Bar' is a verb, not a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bantu are a large group of peoples across central and southern Africa sharing related languages.

clue.text: Go, for example, and get on an elephant?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Go is a strategy contest played on a grid
second meaning: to climb aboard a large wild animal of the kind hunters chase

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go' looks like a verb but is the name of the ancient Asian strategy game. The question mark flags the playful second reading: to board is to get on, and an elephant is big game.
explanation.definitionFit: Go is played with stones on a gridded board, so it is an example of that category; big game means large hunted animals.

clue.text: That's the one thing foxes like — wee

parts.note: urban foxes raid rubbish bins for food
to go is a euphemism for to urinate

explanation.surface: Someone declares that foxes have just one weakness, and it is a small one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wee' looks like the Scottish word for small, but it is the verb for urinating.
explanation.definitionFit: Bingo is an exclamation of sudden success or discovery, much like crying out that you have found the very thing.

clue.text: Endless petanque playing on a road or avenue

indicators.note: something without an end has lost its final part, so the last letter goes

parts.note: petanque is boules, the French bowling game, here missing its last letter
V for versus, as in one side playing another
taken as written
RD is the abbreviation for road

explanation.surface: An endless game of petanque is being played in the street.
explanation.walkthrough: Petanque is also called boules; one side playing another is written V, for versus.
explanation.definitionFit: A boulevard is a broad city street, often tree-lined, so it is a kind of avenue.

clue.text: Cups are moved to the end of counter

indicators.note: moving something to the end takes it out of its place before setting it down at the back

parts.note: a bar is a counter, here losing the letter that moves
A is the symbol for an are, a metric unit of area

explanation.surface: Mugs are shifted to the far end of a kitchen counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Are' is not a verb but the metric unit of a hundred square metres, symbol A.
explanation.definitionFit: A bra consists largely of two shaped cups, so the garment can be cryptically called cups.

clue.text: Naughty children putting smoking paraphernalia in garbage

indicators.note: putting one thing in another sets it inside, so these letters are placed within the others

parts.note: BS is slang for nonsense or rubbish talk
a lighter is used for smoking

explanation.surface: Misbehaving kids are dumping cigarette gear in the rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Garbage' means nonsense talk here, abbreviated as BS.
explanation.definitionFit: Blighter is a mildly disapproving British word for a person, often a mischievous child or rascal.

clue.text: One with cold admitted to A&E

indicators.note: being admitted to a place means being let inside, so one letter goes within the others

parts.note: the letters of the hospital department
C for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A patient with a cold gets admitted to the emergency department.
explanation.walkthrough: A&E, Accident and Emergency, is the British hospital emergency room; the ampersand is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: The ace in a pack of cards counts as one, and on dice the single spot is also called the ace.

clue.text: Building rugby posts alongside river

parts.note: rugby goalposts are shaped like the letter H
the Ouse is an English river

explanation.surface: A rugby ground is being built with its posts beside a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Building' looks like a verb describing construction work, but it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A house is a building people live in, so the general term covers it.

clue.text: Electronic Scrabble letter turned over to make 'CREAM'

indicators.note: turning something over flips it end to end, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: E for electronic, as in e-mail
Scrabble letters are printed on tiles

explanation.surface: In a computer Scrabble game, flipping a tile completes the word CREAM.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals on 'CREAM' make it look like a word played on the board; it is just the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The cream of a group is its best part, and the elite are the best of a group.

clue.text: We gather stupid insinuation is quietening

indicators.note: to gather can mean to hear, as in 'I gather you were away', so the sound counts

parts.note: dim means stupid and an innuendo is an insinuation

explanation.surface: We understand that a foolish hint is calming things down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'We gather' looks like a parenthetical aside, but it is the signal that the two words are heard, not spelt.
explanation.definitionFit: In music, a diminuendo is a gradual decrease in loudness, so it is a quietening.

clue.text: Unit gathered near shelled area

parts.note: to meet is to gather, past tense met

indicators.note: shelling removes the outer casing, so only the inner letters stay

parts.note: the word with its first and last letters removed

explanation.surface: An army unit assembled close to a bombarded zone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shelled' suggests artillery fire, but it means stripped of its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The metre is the base SI measure of length, a standard unit.

clue.text: They like eating bread, nothing special

parts.note: a duck is a score of zero in cricket
S is the abbreviation for special

explanation.surface: Some people enjoy bread with nothing fancy on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nothing special' reads as plain fare, but it splits into two pieces; in cricket a duck is a batsman's score of nil.
explanation.definitionFit: People throw bread to waterfowl at the pond, and these birds eagerly gobble it up.

clue.text: Commonest word/letter for 'you'

parts.note: the is the most frequent word in English
E is the most frequent letter in English, sharing 'commonest'

explanation.surface: A grammar note on the most common way to write 'you'.
explanation.walkthrough: The slash lets 'Commonest' apply to both word and letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Thee is the old object form of the second-person singular pronoun, used in prayers and archaic English.

clue.text: Male and female cycling east of London?

indicators.note: cycling goes round and round, so letters from the front come round to the back

parts.note: male and female are the two sexes

explanation.surface: A man and a woman are out cycling to the east of London.
explanation.walkthrough: Essex is the English county just east of London. Moving the first two letters to the back gives the answer; the question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Essex lies immediately to the east of Greater London, so it is one place that fits that description.

clue.text: Start to drag on Bluebird's joint

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: first letter of drag
Bluebird is the setter, and the setter has is I've

explanation.surface: The setter takes the first drag on their own joint.
explanation.walkthrough: Bluebird is this puzzle's setter, so 'Bluebird's' is 'I've'. 'Drag' and 'joint' suggest smoking cannabis.
explanation.definitionFit: A joint and a dive are both slang for a cheap, seedy bar or nightclub.

clue.text: Perform with a mix of tailless cats

indicators.note: without a tail, the word loses its last letter
a mix jumbles its ingredients, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the word with its final letter removed

explanation.surface: A circus turn starring a motley troupe of cats with no tails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' looks like fodder but belongs to 'a mix of'; tailless cats, such as the Manx breed, really exist, which makes the surface plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: To act is to play a role on stage or screen, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Formality of well-known Greek character with cape

parts.note: a star is a well-known person
chi is a letter of the Greek alphabet
a ness is a headland, as in Orford Ness

explanation.surface: A famous Greek figure in a cloak carries an air of stiff formality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' means a letter of an alphabet, not a person, and 'well-known' must become a noun, star.
explanation.definitionFit: Starchiness is stiff, prim correctness of manner, like a starched collar, so it means formality.

clue.text: Chaotic melees outside the front of rowdy supermarket in Ireland

indicators.note: chaos is disorder, so these letters are thrown out of their order
being outside something surrounds it, so these letters enclose the rest

parts.note: the six letters rearranged

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: first letter of rowdy
Aldi is a discount supermarket chain

explanation.surface: Wild brawls break out in front of a rowdy supermarket in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ireland' sits at the end like a location for the scene, but it is the definition; Aldi is a German discount chain common in Britain and Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Emerald Isle is a poetic nickname for Ireland, from its lush green countryside.

clue.text: Number Ten is suffering setback

indicators.note: a setback sends things backwards, so the letters run in the opposite direction

parts.note: X is ten in Roman numerals
taken as written

explanation.surface: Downing Street, Number Ten, is in trouble after a political setback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number Ten' reads as the Prime Minister's residence in Downing Street, London; 'Number' is in fact the definition and 'Ten' the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Six is a counting number, one more than five, so it is an example of a number.
